claims.text: The eutectic high-entropy alloy has a dual-phase microstructure.
The distinct phases have compositional differences.
The distinct phases have electrochemical differences.
The dual-phase microstructure creates localized galvanic interactions between phases.
The phase-level galvanic couples accelerate anodic dissolution in the less noble phase.
Mechanical wear stress ruptures protective oxide layers.
High local corrosion rates contribute to rupture of protective oxide layers during wear.
Repeated oxide rupture precludes effective oxide-film repair.
The combination of galvanic dissolution and oxide-film rupture accelerates both wear and corrosion degradation.
Under matched elevated-temperature wear-corrosion conditions, the dual-phase alloy will exhibit greater total degradation than a near-single-phase or homogenized control.
The dual-phase alloy will exhibit a higher material-loss rate than the homogeneous control.
The dual-phase alloy will exhibit deeper penetration of corrosive damage than the homogeneous control.
The wear component of degradation will be more severe in the dual-phase alloy than in the homogeneous control.
The corrosion component of degradation will be more severe in the dual-phase alloy than in the homogeneous control.
Elevated-temperature conditions promote oxide formation and stress-induced oxide rupture.
The proposed coupling mechanism is limited to conditions in which mechanical wear and corrosive attack occur simultaneously at temperatures supporting oxide formation and rupture.
Prior literature supports roles for galvanic interactions and oxide rupture in degradation.
